newsitem.title: USA: Top U.S. execs oppose Clinton "de minimis" repeal.
newsitem.headline: Top U.S. execs oppose Clinton "de minimis" repeal.

text.p: Thirty-five top executives from banks and securities firms urged a key U.S. House panel on Thursday to oppose President Clinton's call for repeal of the two percent "de minimis" rule.
President Clinton in his proposed fiscal 1998 federal budget proposed repeal of a series of corporate tax "loopholes" in the U.S. tax code, including the de minimis rule.

"It is ironic that the administration's budget, designed to eliminate the deficit, contains proposals that would have a severe negative effect on investment in the corporate and municipal bond markets," the executives said, in a three-page letter to Rep. Bill Archer, R-Texas, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee.
Among those signing the letter were Kenneth Williams, managing partner of Stone & Youngberg in San Francisco, who is chairman of the municipal bond division of PSA The Bond Market Trade Association.
Other signers include Daniel Tully, chairman of Merrill Lynch & Co; Hardwick Simmons, president of Prudential Securities Inc.; and Richard Fuld, chairman of Lehman Brothers Inc.
Currently, the Internal Revenue Service does not permit businesses to deduct the interest on debt they use to finance the purchase of tax-exempt bonds.

But the Internal Revenue Service in 1972, in what is dubbed the de minimis rule, said that it will not monitor whether a corporation has borrowed to purchase tax-exempt bonds as long as those holdings total less than two percent of a firm's net assets.
